# 12-Week Resistance Training Programme
**Client:** 27F, PCOS (Rotterdam criteria), irregular/anovulatory cycles
**Start date:** 2026-06-01
**Setting:** Full gym access
**Primary aim:** Improve insulin sensitivity, body composition, and strength via progressive resistance training. No cycle-based periodisation given the anovulatory presentation — we'll use a straightforward linear-to-undulating progression with autoregulation via RPE.

---

## Programming Rationale (brief)

- **Resistance training first-line** for PCOS is well-supported: it improves insulin sensitivity independently of weight loss, increases lean mass, and helps with androgen-driven body composition changes.
- **Compound-heavy, moderate-to-high volume** with progressive overload. Prioritise posterior chain, glutes, upper back — muscle groups that carry high metabolic demand and support posture.
- **No cycle syncing.** With cycles ranging 35–90 days and frequent anovulation, luteal/follicular phase periodisation is not viable and evidence is weak even in eumenorrheic women. We use RPE-based autoregulation instead, so she can dial back on low-energy days without derailing the plan.
- **Fatigue management:** PCOS clients often report higher perceived fatigue and sleep disturbance. We cap sessions at 4/week and include a deload.
- **Zone 2 cardio** is added as a metabolic health adjunct — not for calorie burn, but for mitochondrial and insulin-sensitivity benefit. Kept low so it doesn't compete with recovery.

---

## Weekly Structure

**4 resistance sessions + 2 low-intensity cardio + 1 full rest**

- **Mon:** Lower A (squat-focused)
- **Tue:** Upper A (push-focused) + 20–30 min Zone 2
- **Wed:** Rest or mobility
- **Thu:** Lower B (hinge-focused)
- **Fri:** Upper B (pull-focused) + 20–30 min Zone 2
- **Sat:** Optional Zone 2 walk (30–45 min) or off
- **Sun:** Rest

**RPE guidance:** Target RPE 7–8 on working sets (2–3 reps in reserve). Warm-ups not counted in set totals.

---

## PHASE 1 — Foundation & Movement Quality (Weeks 1–4)

Goal: establish technique, build baseline work capacity, moderate loads. Higher reps (8–12) to build tissue tolerance and confidence under the bar.

### Week 1 — Introduction (RPE 6–7)

**Lower A**
- Goblet squat — 3×10
- Romanian deadlift (dumbbell) — 3×10
- Walking lunge — 2×10/leg
- Hip thrust (bodyweight or barbell light) — 3×12
- Plank — 3×30s

**Upper A**
- DB bench press — 3×10
- Seated cable row — 3×10
- DB shoulder press — 3×10
- Lat pulldown — 3×10
- Cable triceps pushdown — 2×12

**Lower B**
- Trap-bar deadlift — 3×8 (technique focus)
- Bulgarian split squat — 3×8/leg
- Leg curl — 3×12
- Cable pull-through — 3×12
- Dead bug — 3×10/side

**Upper B**
- Chest-supported row — 3×10
- Incline DB press — 3×10
- Lat pulldown (neutral grip) — 3×10
- Face pull — 3×15
- DB curl — 2×12

### Week 2 — Add load (RPE 7)
Same template. Add 2.5–5 kg where technique allows. Add one set to main compound lifts (squat, RDL, deadlift, bench, row → 4 sets).

### Week 3 — Progress (RPE 7–8)
- Goblet squat → **Barbell back squat** 4×8
- DB bench → **Barbell bench** 4×8
- Trap-bar DL → 4×6
- Chest-supported row → 4×8
- Add barbell hip thrust 3×10 on Lower A

### Week 4 — Consolidation (RPE 7)
Hold loads from Week 3; focus on bar path, tempo (3s eccentric on all compounds this week). Test 8-rep working sets on squat, bench, deadlift, row to establish baselines.

---

## PHASE 2 — Strength & Hypertrophy Build (Weeks 5–8)

Goal: shift toward heavier compounds (5–8 reps) with continued accessory volume for hypertrophy. Undulating rep ranges within the week.

### Weekly Template

**Lower A (heavy squat day)**
- Back squat — 4×6 @ RPE 7–8
- Romanian deadlift — 3×8
- Barbell hip thrust — 3×8
- Leg press — 3×12
- Cable crunch — 3×12

**Upper A (heavy press day)**
- Bench press — 4×6
- Overhead press — 3×8
- Chest-supported row — 3×10
- Lateral raise — 3×15
- Triceps pushdown — 3×12

**Lower B (heavy hinge day)**
- Trap-bar or conventional deadlift — 4×5
- Front-foot elevated split squat — 3×8/leg
- Seated leg curl — 3×10
- Back extension — 3×12
- Pallof press — 3×10/side

**Upper B (hypertrophy pull)**
- Pull-up (assisted as needed) — 4×6–8
- Incline DB press — 3×10
- Seated cable row — 3×10
- Face pull — 3×15
- Hammer curl — 3×10

### Progression Weeks 5→8
- **Week 5:** Establish loads at RPE 7.
- **Week 6:** Add 2.5 kg to main lifts (squat, bench, DL, press).
- **Week 7:** Push to RPE 8; add 1 set to squat and deadlift (5 sets).
- **Week 8 (deload):** Reduce sets by ~40% and load by ~20%. Keep movement patterns. 2×5 on main lifts at RPE 6. Extra sleep, extra mobility.

---

## PHASE 3 — Strength Expression & Density (Weeks 9–12)

Goal: peak strength on core lifts, keep hypertrophy accessories, introduce more challenging unilateral and metabolic work.

### Weekly Template

**Lower A**
- Back squat — 5×4 @ RPE 8
- Barbell hip thrust — 4×6
- Front squat or safety-bar squat — 3×6
- Walking lunge with DBs — 3×8/leg
- Hanging knee raise — 3×10

**Upper A**
- Bench press — 5×4 @ RPE 8
- Weighted dip or close-grip bench — 3×6
- Pendlay row — 3×6
- DB shoulder press — 3×8
- Lateral raise — 3×15

**Lower B**
- Deadlift — 4×3 @ RPE 8
- Deficit RDL — 3×8
- Bulgarian split squat — 3×8/leg
- Nordic curl (assisted) or seated leg curl — 3×8
- Suitcase carry — 3×30m/side

**Upper B**
- Weighted pull-up — 4×5
- Incline barbell press — 4×6
- Chest-supported row — 4×8
- Face pull — 3×15
- Barbell or EZ curl — 3×8

### Weeks 9–12 progression
- **Week 9:** Introduce heavier rep ranges (5×4, 4×3), RPE 8.
- **Week 10:** Add small load increment on main lifts. Add 1 top set at RPE 8.5 on squat and deadlift.
- **Week 11:** Peak week. Work up to a heavy triple on squat, bench, and deadlift (~RPE 8.5–9). Back-off sets at 80% of top set.
- **Week 12:** Retest 5RM on squat, bench, deadlift, and 8RM row. Session volume reduced across the rest of the week (mini-deload leading in, light accessories after testing).

---

## Cardio Component

- **Zone 2 (conversational pace, ~60–70% HRmax):** 2×20–30 min in Phases 1–2, extending to 2×30–40 min in Phase 3. Bike, incline treadmill walk, or elliptical.
- **NEAT target:** 7,000–9,000 steps/day. This matters more than programmed cardio for PCOS-related metabolic outcomes.
- **Avoid HIIT** in this block. It's a viable tool later but adds fatigue and cortisol load we don't need while establishing consistency.

---

## Nutrition Notes (share with client's dietitian if she has one)

I'd defer specific macros to a dietitian familiar with PCOS, but general principles that support the programme:

- **Protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg bodyweight/day.** Non-negotiable for recovery and satiety, and particularly useful given insulin resistance.
- **Prioritise protein + fibre at each meal** to blunt glycaemic response.
- **Carbohydrate timing:** most carbs around training sessions supports performance and may improve insulin utilisation.
- **Avoid aggressive deficits** in Weeks 1–4. Establish training first. If fat loss is a goal, a modest deficit (~10–15%) can begin Phase 2.
- **Inositol (myo + d-chiro, 40:1) and vitamin D** are commonly used in PCOS — refer to her endocrinologist.

---

## Recovery & Autoregulation

- **Sleep target: 7.5–9 h.** Sleep disruption is common in PCOS and directly impairs insulin sensitivity. Flag this at every check-in.
- **RPE rule:** if warm-ups feel like RPE 8, drop the working weight by 10% that session and continue. Don't skip.
- **Track:** morning resting HR, session RPE, and a subjective 1–10 energy score. Two consecutive days of RHR >7 bpm above baseline or energy <4 → swap a resistance day for mobility/walk.
- **Menstrual tracking:** log any bleed and its character. Not for programming — for her medical team and to spot changes over the 12 weeks.
- **Deload:** Week 8 as scheduled. If she reports high fatigue in Weeks 6 or 10, insert an unscheduled deload rather than pushing through.

---

## Progress Metrics (test Week 1 baseline, retest Week 12)

- 5RM: back squat, bench press, deadlift
- 8RM: chest-supported row
- Bodyweight, waist circumference, hip circumference (weekly, same conditions)
- Optional: DEXA or bioimpedance at Week 0 and Week 12
- Subjective: energy, sleep quality, mood, cycle changes

Let me know if you'd like me to expand the warm-ups, add exercise substitutions in case equipment is busy, or build a follow-on Phase 4.

# Nutrition Plan — PCOS, Insulin Sensitivity Focus

**Client:** 27F, PCOS
**Alignment:** 12-week resistance programme starting 2026-06-01
**Non-negotiable:** No aggressive deficit, no fasted training, no skipped meals. Under-fuelling worsens PCOS via elevated cortisol, disrupted LH/FSH signalling, poorer recovery, and rebound hyperphagia. We're building metabolic health, not chasing scale weight.

> **Scope note:** This is a training-support nutrition framework, not medical nutrition therapy. If she has a registered dietitian, defer to them on medication interactions, specific supplement dosing, and any comorbidities (thyroid, lipids, NAFLD, etc.).

---

## Guiding Principles

1. **Eat enough.** Energy availability first, everything else second.
2. **Protein at every meal.** Blunts glycaemic response, supports lean mass, high satiety.
3. **Fibre at every meal.** Slows gastric emptying, feeds gut microbiome, improves post-meal glucose.
4. **Fat + protein + fibre before or with carbs** — never carbs alone, especially at breakfast.
5. **Consistent meal timing.** 3 meals + 1–2 snacks. No long gaps, no skipped breakfast.
6. **Carbs earn their place around training.** Not restricted — strategically placed.
7. **Whole-food carbs default.** Refined carbs are fine occasionally, not as staples.

---

## Energy Intake

**Do not calorie-cut in Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4).** Eat at estimated maintenance while she builds training capacity and we see how she responds. Under-eating in a PCOS client with a new training stimulus is the fastest way to stall progress and worsen symptoms.

**Estimating maintenance** (adjust to her stats):

- Sedentary BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor) × 1.5–1.6 activity factor for 4 lifting sessions + walking
- For a typical 27F at ~68 kg, ~165 cm: roughly **2,100–2,300 kcal/day** at maintenance.
- **Re-weigh weekly**, same conditions. If bodyweight is stable ±0.5 kg over 2–3 weeks, that's her maintenance.

**Phase 2–3 (Weeks 5–12), if fat loss is a goal:**

- Modest deficit only: **10–15% below maintenance**, never more.
- Floor: **no less than 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day.** Below this, energy availability drops and PCOS symptoms typically worsen.
- **Diet break every 3–4 weeks:** 5–7 days at maintenance. This isn't a treat — it's programmed to protect thyroid function, leptin, and cycle recovery.
- If bodyweight, mood, sleep, or gym performance drop for 2 consecutive weeks → return to maintenance immediately.

**Red flags to stop the deficit:**
- Loss of morning erections of energy (persistent fatigue >1 week)
- Sleep quality drops
- Gym performance regresses 2 sessions in a row
- Increased cravings, binge urges
- Cycle disappears entirely (if it was appearing)
- Resting HR climbs and stays elevated

---

## Macros

**Protein — non-negotiable priority:**
- **1.8–2.2 g/kg bodyweight/day** (~120–150 g for 68 kg)
- Distribute across 4 feedings: ~30–40 g per meal/snack
- Sources: eggs, Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, chicken, fish, lean beef, tofu, tempeh, whey/casein

**Carbohydrates — moderate, strategic:**
- **3–4 g/kg/day** (~200–270 g for 68 kg) on training days
- **2.5–3 g/kg/day** on rest days
- Bulk of daily carbs in the pre- and post-training meals
- Lower-carb at breakfast and evening meals if not adjacent to training
- **Sources:** oats, potatoes, sweet potato, rice, quinoa, lentils, beans, chickpeas, fruit (especially berries), whole-grain sourdough. Minimise: sugary drinks, refined pastries, ultra-processed snacks — not because "sugar is evil" but because they spike glucose without satiety.

**Fat — sufficient, not restrictive:**
- **0.8–1.0 g/kg/day** (~55–70 g for 68 kg)
- Emphasise mono- and polyunsaturated: olive oil, avocado, nuts, seeds, oily fish
- **Omega-3 rich:** salmon, sardines, mackerel 2–3×/week (or supplement, see below)

**Fibre:**
- **Target 30–40 g/day.** This is one of the single most impactful levers for insulin sensitivity in PCOS.
- Build via: vegetables at 2 meals, legumes 4–5×/week, berries, oats, chia/flax, whole grains.

---

## Meal Timing Around Training

Sessions are Mon (Lower A), Tue (Upper A), Thu (Lower B), Fri (Upper B).

**Pre-training (60–90 min before):**
- 30–40 g protein + 40–60 g carbs + low fat/fibre
- Example: Greek yoghurt + banana + honey + whey scoop, or chicken + rice + small salad

**Post-training (within 60–90 min):**
- 30–40 g protein + 60–80 g carbs + vegetables
- Example: salmon + potatoes + roasted veg, or lean beef stir-fry with rice

**Rest days:**
- Same protein target
- Carbs pulled slightly lower and distributed evenly
- Extra vegetables and fats

---

## Sample Day — Training Day (~2,200 kcal, ~140 g protein, ~240 g carbs, ~65 g fat, ~35 g fibre)

**Breakfast (07:30)**
- 3 whole eggs + 2 egg whites scrambled
- 1 slice whole-grain sourdough
- ½ avocado
- Handful of berries
- Coffee or tea

**Mid-morning snack (10:30)**
- Greek yoghurt (200 g, 0% or 2%) + 20 g mixed nuts + cinnamon

**Pre-training meal (12:30, training at 14:00)**
- Chicken breast (150 g) + white rice (80 g dry) + cucumber/tomato salad + olive oil

**Post-training meal (16:00)**
- Salmon (150 g) + roasted potatoes (300 g) + big serving of roasted vegetables + tahini drizzle

**Dinner (19:30)**
- Lentil and vegetable soup with cottage cheese on the side, or turkey and bean chilli with a small side salad

**Optional evening (if hungry):**
- Casein or Greek yoghurt + berries + chia

---

## Sample Day — Rest Day (~2,000 kcal, ~135 g protein, ~180 g carbs, ~75 g fat, ~40 g fibre)

Drop pre-/post-training carbs, redistribute:

**Breakfast:** Same as training day
**Snack:** Same
**Lunch:** Big mixed salad — chicken, chickpeas, feta, olives, quinoa (60 g dry), olive oil, lemon
**Snack:** Apple + 2 tbsp nut butter
**Dinner:** Steak (150 g) + sweet potato + sautéed greens + avocado

---

## Specific PCOS Considerations

**Breakfast matters more than in the general population.**
Skipping breakfast in PCOS is associated with worsened insulin and androgen profiles. Even on days she's not hungry, aim for at least a protein + fat mini-meal (e.g. Greek yoghurt + nuts) within 90 min of waking.

**Order of eating.**
Practical trick with real evidence: eat protein and vegetables/fibre *first*, starches/sugars *last* within a meal. Meaningfully lowers post-meal glucose.

**Post-meal movement.**
10–15 min walk after the largest meal of the day. Cheap, effective, no downside.

**Alcohol.**
Ideally minimal. If she drinks, cap at 1–2 units, with food, not on training days. Alcohol impairs recovery and worsens sleep quality.

**Caffeine.**
Fine, keep it before 14:00 given PCOS-related sleep vulnerability.

- **No spinal flexion or hinging under load.** No RDLs, no good mornings, no bent-over rows.
- **No Valsalva under heavy load.** Increased intra-abdominal pressure is unhelpful here.

# Flare Recovery Framework — Irregular Cycle Context

Given we have no reliable cycle projection, we can't pre-programme recovery around predicted flares. Instead, we build a **responsive system**: default programming runs as planned, and flares trigger a defined protocol when they occur. Over time, tracked data may reveal patterns we can eventually programme *toward*.

---

## Core Principle

**Treat flares as unscheduled deloads, not setbacks.** The programme is designed with enough flexibility that 1–2 flare weeks per 12-week block cost her almost nothing in long-term progress. What *does* cost her progress: pushing through flares, panic-cutting calories during them, or trying to "make up" missed sessions afterward.

---

## The Flare Response Ladder

A tiered protocol based on severity. She and the trainer classify the flare on Day 1, then follow the matching tier. Can be upgraded or downgraded across the flare — this isn't locked in.

### Tier 1 — Mild Flare
*Symptoms: low-grade pain, mild fatigue, mood or bloating symptoms, no significant back or joint involvement. Function largely intact.*

- **Training:** continue as programmed, drop RPE cap to 6 for the week
- **Volume:** reduce sets by ~20% on main lifts (e.g. 4×6 becomes 3×6)
- **Cardio:** swap moderate sessions for Zone 2
- **Nutrition:** unchanged, maintenance
- **Duration to trigger next tier:** if not resolving in 3 days, move to Tier 2

### Tier 2 — Moderate Flare
*Symptoms: notable pain, disrupted sleep, meaningful fatigue, mild back involvement, or heavy bleeding with cramping.*

- **Training:** pause lower-body barbell work. Upper body sessions permitted, seated/supported preferred. RPE cap 6.
- **Substitute lower days** with: machine-based lower work (leg press, leg curl, leg extension) OR mobility + walking sessions
- **Cardio:** walking only, or gentle bike Zone 2
- **Nutrition:** maintenance. Extra protein, omega-3, hydration. Consider magnesium in the evening.
- **Duration to trigger next tier:** worsening symptoms, or lasting >4 days

### Tier 3 — Severe Flare (like the late-June event)
*Symptoms: significant pain, lower-back inflammation, heavy bleeding, unable to train through it.*

- **Training:** suspend gym sessions entirely
- **Movement:** gentle walking 2–3× short bouts daily, gentle mobility (cat-cow, child's pose, 90/90 breathing, supine knee hugs)
- **Cardio:** none beyond walking
- **Nutrition:** maintenance, do not cut. Anti-inflammatory emphasis (fatty fish, berries, leafy greens, turmeric, olive oil). No alcohol.
- **Sleep:** absolute priority — 8+ hours, dark room, cool temperature
- **Duration to trigger escalation:** if symptoms lasting >5 days or worsening despite rest, this becomes a medical conversation, not a training one. Loop in her endocrinologist.

---

## Return-to-Training Protocol (all tiers)

**The bridge week is non-negotiable after Tier 2 or Tier 3.** After Tier 1, resume normal programming.

### Bridge session structure (first session back)
- Cap duration at 30 min
- All exercises at ~50–60% of pre-flare working load
- RPE ceiling: 6
- No max effort sets, no new PRs, no "testing" how she feels

### Bridge week (Tier 2/3 return)
- 3 sessions rather than 4
- All main lifts at 50–60% of pre-flare loads, RPE 6–7
- Full accessory work at moderate loads
- One moderate cardio session at the light end (20 min bike, RPE 5)
- Skip the second moderate cardio session

### Green lights to resume full programming (checklist)
- No symptoms during or 24h after the bridge sessions
- Sleep back to baseline for 3+ consecutive nights
- Energy score 7+/10
- Bridge loads felt controlled, no compensatory movement patterns
- No morning stiffness above baseline

If any green light is missing → run the bridge week again with a small load bump. **Do not skip the bridge to catch up.**

---

## Programming the Programme Around Uncertainty

Since we can't predict flares, we build the block to *absorb* them:

**1. Front-load nothing critical.**
Retest weeks and peak weeks (Week 11–12 in the current block) are the only sessions that "must" happen on a specific day. Everything else can shift by ±3 days without meaningful cost.

**2. Deload week placement stays flexible.**
Week 8 is the scheduled deload. If a Tier 2+ flare hits in Weeks 6 or 7, we skip the scheduled deload and continue — the flare *was* the deload. If flares hit Weeks 9 or 10, we may need to pull the peak week or extend the block.

**3. Build in a buffer week.**
For future 12-week blocks, I'd recommend programming for 11 weeks of work and holding Week 12 as a flex week — either a retest week if she's had a clean run, or absorbed as needed if she's had 1–2 flares. Removes the pressure to "hit the schedule."

**4. Weekly session count is a target, not a rule.**
The programme is written as 4 lifting + 2 cardio. The floor is **2 lifting sessions per week**. Below that, we're detraining. Above that in flare weeks, we're overreaching. Two quality sessions in a flare week protects the training adaptation.

---

## What to Track (this is where the payoff is)

The main long-game move: build a flare log that eventually gives us predictive information her endocrinologist doesn't currently have.

**Each flare, log:**
- Date, duration, severity 1–10
- Symptom profile (pain location, bleeding, mood, fatigue, GI, sleep)
- Bleeding association: was there a bleed in the 7 days before, during, or after?
- Training load in the 7 days prior (session count, total tonnage, RPE average)
- Sleep average (previous 7 nights)
- Stress rating (life stress, 1–10, previous 7 days)
- Nutrition adherence (previous 7 days, %)
- Menstrual notes (any bleeding, spotting, discharge changes)

**Weekly baseline (independent of flares):**
- Morning resting HR
- Sleep quality and duration
- Energy, mood, hunger
- Bodyweight (7-day average)
- Any bleeding

**After 6+ months of this data**, patterns often emerge:
- Flares clustering with (or independently of) bleeds
- Flares following high-stress weeks
- Flares following poor sleep runs
- Flares following training spikes

Once patterns emerge, we can start *anticipating* — e.g. "post-bleed weeks tend to be flare-prone, so we programme lower volume there." But we don't guess at this now. **6 months of data before pattern-based programming decisions.**

---

## Nutrition During and After Flares

Repeating because it's the most commonly-broken rule:

**Never cut calories during a flare.** Even if she's not training, energy needs are elevated by inflammation, and under-fuelling extends recovery time and worsens the next cycle's flare probability.

**During flare:**
- Maintenance calories
- Protein target unchanged (1.8–2.2 g/kg)
- Emphasise anti-inflammatory foods: fatty fish, berries, leafy greens, olive oil, nuts, turmeric, ginger
- Extra hydration (+500 ml/day)
- Magnesium glycinate evening if cramping or sleep disruption
- No alcohol
- Coffee: fine, but not on empty stomach

**Post-flare bridge week:**
- Return to normal training-day/rest-day macro split
- Slight protein bump (~2.2 g/kg) during the bridge week to support tissue recovery
- Do not attempt to "make up" for missed training deficit — that ship has sailed and chasing it is counterproductive

---

## Communication Framework

Simple 3-question check-in whenever she reports symptoms:

1. **Pain or symptom severity right now, 1–10?**
2. **Can you walk 10 minutes comfortably?**
3. **Did you sleep last night?**

- All three green (≤4, yes, yes) → Tier 1
- One or two flags → Tier 2
- Two or three flags, or severity 7+ → Tier 3

Fast, unambiguous, keeps decisions off vibes.

---

## When to Involve Her Medical Team

Flag to her endocrinologist (not for us to manage) if:
- Flare frequency increases across the programme
- Flare severity trends up
- New symptoms emerge (particularly severe pelvic pain, changes in bleeding pattern, new joint involvement)
- Any flare lasting >7 days
- Pattern of flares independent of bleeding that we can't explain

Our role is training and recovery within her medical picture — not diagnosing or managing PCOS itself. The tracking data we're building becomes useful information for her endocrinology team as well.

---

## Bottom Line for the Client

She's not fragile, and flares are not failures. The programme is built to bend around them. What matters over 12 weeks — and over the next year — is total consistent training volume, not any single week. A client who trains 40 out of 48 weeks with intelligent flare management will progress dramatically more than one who trains 48 weeks by pushing through symptoms and accumulating setbacks.

# Cycle-Aware Programming Update

**Great news clinically.** Return to regular ovulatory cycles is a meaningful marker of improved metabolic health in PCOS — often reflects better insulin sensitivity, reduced androgen load, and improved HPO axis function. Worth flagging to her endocrinologist as a positive response.

## A Note on the Evidence

Cycle-based training periodisation has weaker evidence than social media suggests. The best-supported observations:

- **Follicular phase** (post-bleed → ovulation): higher pain tolerance, better recovery, often peak strength expression
- **Ovulation window:** peak performance for many, but slightly elevated injury risk (relaxin effects, though modest)
- **Luteal phase** (post-ovulation → next bleed): higher perceived exertion, worse sleep, elevated core temp, greater fatigue in the late luteal
- **Menstrual phase:** highly individual — some feel strong, some flatten

**How we use this:** as *soft* biasing, not rigid rules. We schedule the hardest work when she's most likely to recover well, and pull back when she's likely to feel worse. We don't refuse to lift heavy in the luteal phase — we just don't peak there if we have the choice.

**We calibrate to *her*, not the textbook.** First cycle on this system, we log symptoms and performance daily. Real data beats theoretical phase models every time.

## The Cycle-Aware Weekly Template

Same 4 lifting + 2 cardio structure. What changes is **which day within the week carries the heaviest load**, matched to phase.

### Menstrual Phase (Days 1–5)

**Bias:** Autoregulate. Some clients feel strong here, some flat. Programme normally but drop RPE cap to 7 and allow her to swap a heavy day for a moderate day if she reports low energy.

- Mon Lower A — RPE 7 cap
- Tue Upper A + Zone 2
- Wed Moderate cardio *or* rest if flow is heavy
- Thu Lower B — RPE 7 cap
- Fri Upper B + Zone 2
- Sat Zone 2 or optional
- Sun Rest

**Iron consideration:** heavier bleeds increase iron demand. Emphasise iron-rich foods (red meat, lentils, spinach + vitamin C source) during and just after menses. Flag to her endocrinologist if she hasn't had ferritin checked recently.

### Follicular Phase (Days 6–13) — **Push Phase**

**Bias:** This is when we programme the heaviest, most demanding work. Highest tolerance for volume and intensity, best recovery, peak strength expression for most women.

- Mon Lower A — **top-set day, RPE 8**, hit heaviest working sets of the mesocycle here
- Tue Upper A + moderate cardio
- Wed Moderate cardio (Format B — cruise intervals appropriate here)
- Thu Lower B — heavy hinge, RPE 8
- Fri Upper B + Zone 2
- Sat Moderate cardio 35–40 min
- Sun Rest

**This is where PRs happen.** If we're testing 5RMs or hitting peak weeks, schedule them into the follicular window whenever possible.

### Ovulation Window (Days 14–16) — **Peak, then ease**

**Bias:** Peak performance possible here, but joint laxity is modestly elevated. Fine to lift heavy on stable lifts (bench, press, machine work) — be more conservative on high-skill, high-load lifts like heavy singles or maximal deadlifts.

- Continue programming as follicular but drop max-effort singles from lifts requiring peak stability
- Otherwise train normally

### Early Luteal (Days 17–22) — **Maintain**

**Bias:** Still a strong training window. Some progesterone-driven fatigue creeping in, slightly elevated core temp, sleep may start to shift. Full programming continues, RPE 7–8 fine.

- Mon Lower A — normal load, RPE 7–8
- Tue Upper A + Zone 2
- Wed Moderate cardio
- Thu Lower B — normal load
- Fri Upper B + Zone 2
- Sat Zone 2 or moderate (by feel)
- Sun Rest

### Late Luteal / PMS Window (Days 23–28) — **Pull Back**

**Bias:** This is where the programme should soften. Elevated perceived exertion, poorer sleep quality, higher core temp, more inflammation, mood dips. Pushing hard here often means worse-quality work *and* worse recovery for the same effort.

- Mon Lower A — **RPE 7 cap**, drop 1 set from main lifts, reduce load by ~5–10%
- Tue Upper A + Zone 2 (skip moderate cardio if fatigue is high)
- Wed Zone 2 only, not moderate

# 12-Week Programme — Full Re-emission with Cycle-Aware Scheduling

**Client:** 27F, PCOS (Rotterdam), cycle now regularised
**Cycle anchor:** Day 1 = 2026-05-03, 28-day length
**Programme start:** 2026-06-01
**Programme end (revised):** 2026-09-06 (extended by 2 weeks to align retest with follicular phase)
**Setting:** Full gym

---

## Programming Philosophy (summary)

- Resistance training as first-line intervention for PCOS: insulin sensitivity, body composition, androgen management
- Cycle-aware scheduling from Week 6 onward (once we had confirmed regularity)
- Weeks 1–5 delivered pre-cycle-awareness and stand as executed, including flare-modified Week 4 and bridge Week 5
- Retest shifted from Week 12 to Week 14 to land in follicular phase of Cycle 5
- No under-fuelling under any circumstance
- Flare tiers and return-to-training bridge protocols carried through the block

---

## Cycle Map Across the Programme

| Prog Week | Dates | Cycle Phase Covered | Programming Bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jun 1–7 | Cycle 2: menses end → follicular | (pre-cycle-aware) foundation |
| 2 | Jun 8–14 | Cycle 2: follicular → ovulation | (pre-cycle-aware) foundation |
| 3 | Jun 15–21 | Cycle 2: ovulation → early luteal | (pre-cycle-aware) foundation |
| 4 | Jun 22–28 | Cycle 2: late luteal → menses | **Flare-modified recovery** |
| 5 | Jun 29 – Jul 5 | Cycle 3: menses → follicular | **Bridge week** |
| 6 | Jul 6–12 | Cycle 3: follicular → ovulation | **Push — heaviest work** |

| 13 | Aug 24–30 | Cycle 5: menses → follicular | **Peak prep** |
| 14 | Aug 31 – Sep 6 | Cycle 5: mid-follicular | **Retest week** |

---

## Standing Weekly Structure

- **Mon:** Lower A
- **Tue:** Upper A + Zone 2 cardio (20–30 min)
- **Wed:** Moderate cardio (25–35 min) — non-impact modality preferred
- **Thu:** Lower B
- **Fri:** Upper B + Zone 2 cardio (20–30 min)
- **Sat:** Moderate cardio (30–40 min) or long Zone 2 walk
- **Sun:** Rest

**Every lower-body session pre-primed with:** dead bug 1×8/side, side plank 1×20s/side, Pallof press 1×8/side. Permanent addition post-flare.

**Autoregulation rule:** RPE targets are ceilings. If warm-ups feel like RPE 8, reduce working load by 10% that session.

---

# PHASE 1 — Foundation (Weeks 1–4)

Goal: technique, tissue tolerance, baseline capacity. Higher reps (8–12), lower intensity, learn the movements.
